In particular, I don't seem to be able to show that (f∙())∙g=f∙(()∙g)(\mathbf{f} \bullet ()) \bullet \mathbf{g} = \mathbf{f} \bullet (() \bullet \mathbf{g}) (f∙())∙g=f∙(()∙g), where f\mathbf{f}f and g\mathbf{g}g are suitably typed sequences. ...I think I've managed to unconfuse myself. In particular, (fi∙())∙g=fi∙()(f_i \bullet ()) \bullet \mathbf{g} = f_i \bullet ()(fi​∙())∙g=fi​∙() is, in fact, an instance of the associativity axiom for clones.

I would still appreciate a standard reference :)

I'm not completely sure what you mean by abstract clones with multiple colours, but I suspect I don't know of a standard reference for those. Wrt ordinary abstract clones: There is an equivalence of categories between abstract clones and "single-sorted finite product theories", that is, small categories in which all objects are finite products of a single object. This appears in the appendix of:

Taylor, W. Characterizing Mal’cev conditions. Algebra Universalis 3 (1973), 351–397.

The only proper textbook account of abstract clones that I am aware of is Chapter 10 of:

Freese, R. S., McKenzie, R. N., McNulty, G. F., and Taylor, W. F. Algebras, Lattices, Varieties Volume III, 1 ed., vol. 269 of Mathematical Surveys and Monographs. American Mathematical Society, Providence, 2022.

It's aimed at general (universal) algebraists and might be said to be a bit categorist unfriendly---they don't generally allow nullary operations in clones, though they do tell the reader how to include them in Ex. 10.8.16.

Hope this helps :)
Thanks!

I assumed "with multiple colors" is a synonym for "multisorted", so that "abstract clones with multiple colors" is another way of thinking about "multisorted Lawvere theories and their algebras", which in turn is a synonym for cartesian categories where all objects are products of a chosen set of objects {xi}i∈X\{x_i\}_{i \in X}{xi​}i∈X​, and product-preserving functors from these to SetX\mathsf{Set}^XSetX, where xix_ixi​ gets mapped to the ith set in an object of SetX\mathsf{Set}^XSetX.

I'm not very familiar with the "clone" terminology, so I'm not sure if the clone is supposed to be the theory or its category of algebras.
Something like that, yes. In my head the correctness criterion for a notion of "multicoloured abstract clone" is that it's the same thing as a cartesian multicategory (but presented differently).
... I'm pretty sure "abstract clone" always refers to the theory, not the algebras.
Abstract clone always refers to the theory, yes.
I'm quite familiar with the single-sorted version but not the multi-sorted version.
Is there some reason to disallow nullary operations?
Well... the short answer is no.
@Nathanael Arkor might know of some sort of standard reference on multi-sorted abstract clones...

Another standard reference for (one-sorted) abstract clones is Walter Taylor “Abstract Clone Theory”. In: Algebras and Orders. Ed. by Ivo G. Rosenberg and Gert Sabidussi. Kluwer Academic Publisher, 1993, pp. 507–530

I'm not sure of a comprehensive reference, but @Philip Saville's Clones, closed categories, and combinatory logic covers some of the basic theory (though not quite the 2-adjunction you are looking for).

The thing I'm confused about has to do with empty sequences.

It's perhaps worth noting that clones are also commonly defined without nullary operations in the universal algebra world. E.g. in this introductory paper they do this and say the following:

If we're thinking about clones as models of programming languages, however, it seems to me that we do generally want to talk about closed constants so it's worth keeping them in.
I think if you want a nice adjunction relating clones to categories with (strict) finite products, then you probably have to consider nullary operations.
Also your link just points to "categorytheory.zulipchat.com"
Maybe we should come up with a different name for the multicoloured, nullary-operations-allowed version of a clone...
"Projectoid" ^^

In my opinion, the exclusion of nullary operations by algebraists is not sufficient reason to choose a different name for single-sorted clones at least, and is not even universal among algebraists---see Clones with Nullary Operations.

I might be considered biased because of my current work on concrete clones (with nullary operations). If one were to divorce the nullary from non-nullary versions, the term "concrete clone" would lose meaningfulness and a great deal of historical context dating back to the work of Emil Post in the 1920s. I imagine one could also study multi-sorted concrete clones. So I favour the name multi-sorted abstract clones.
@Chad Nester Yes, you lose the empty product if you exclude nullaries.

@Chad Nester You might find it worth taking a look at Richard Garner's Lawvere theories, finitary monads and Cauchy-completion. If I'm understanding it correctly, he explicitly connects "a many-object version" of abstract clones and certain cartesian multicategories across Remarks 3.2 and 3.3.
Thanks for the references!
